01.event: Rabbi Zakkai recited a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan classifying the area between the side posts and beneath the cross beam as a karmelit.
01.outcome: He told Rabbi Zakkai to go and teach it outside the study hall.
01.summary: Rabbi Zakkai recited a teaching before Rabbi Yochanan: the area between the side posts and under the cross beam of an alleyway has the status of a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan dismissed it, telling him to go out and teach it outside, meaning it did not belong in the study hall.

02.actor: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
02.event: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua found the Sages in Rav's study hall arguing that halla is a Torah obligation today even if teruma is rabbinic.
02.turn: He told them the opposite: even if teruma is Torah law, halla is rabbinic, citing a baraita about 'when you come into the land'.
02.outcome: His argument concludes that in Ezra's time not all the people ascended, so halla was not restored as a Torah obligation; no reaction from the Sages is told.
02.summary: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua recounts that he came upon the Sages in Rav's study hall, who were saying that halla is a Torah obligation today even if teruma is not. He countered that the reverse holds, because the obligation applies only when all of Israel enters the land, and in Ezra's day not everyone came up. The incident is only a frame for a legal argument.
02.missing: Any reaction or resolution from the Sages; the content is legal argument rather than events.

03.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
03.event: A man whose brother died faced levirate marriage with the widow, and his brother wanted to disqualify her from him by giving her a bill of divorce.
03.turn: The man offered to share the estate; the brother feared being cheated as the Pumbedita swindler had done, so the man offered to let him take his share immediately.
03.outcome: The passage ends with the offer; whether the brother accepted or what happened is not told.
03.summary: In Mata Mehasya a man was due to take his late brother's widow in levirate marriage, but another brother wanted to disqualify her by divorce. The man asked why, and offered to split the dead brother's property. The brother said he feared being swindled as the Pumbedita trickster had done, so the man offered to let him take his share right away.
03.missing: The outcome: whether the offer was accepted and the levirate marriage went ahead.

04.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa
04.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
04.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
04.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, which the Gemara says was beyond the letter of the law.
04.summary: A man sold a field to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. When it turned out he no longer needed the money, Rav Pappa gave him back his land. The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa did this out of generosity, beyond what the law required.

05.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee and a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori
05.event: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a poor man of good family a litra of meat every day.
05.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee provided a poor man of noble family from Tzippori with a litra of meat every day. The Gemara explains why this was remarkable: it was costly poultry, or they paid a litra of coins, or, as Rav Ashi says, in their small village they slaughtered a whole animal each day just for him.
05.missing: A turn or ending; this describes an ongoing practice of charity rather than an event that develops.

06.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from the field he worked.
06.turn: When he came before Rava, Rava asked who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen.
06.outcome: The betrothal was invalid; the Gemara adds that with a whole bundle it would have been different.
06.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his landlord's field to betroth a woman, then came to Rava about it. Rava asked him who had allowed him to take them: the onions were not his, so the betrothal did not take effect. The Gemara notes that a whole bundle would be different, since he could claim it as his share of the crop.

07.event: According to the judges of Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda decided a case involving bundles of vine branches.
07.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda once ruled in a case about bundles of vine branches. The text gives only the bare report, and then ties it to his general view that eating even forbidden produce from land counts as taking possession of it.
07.missing: The facts of the case and the ruling itself; the Hebrew gives only that he acted in a case of bundles of branches (the translation supplies the details).

09.event: People came before Rabbi Ami with a bill of divorce that needed more witnesses.
09.outcome: He told them to go and complete it even with a slave from the marketplace.
09.summary: A case was brought to Rabbi Ami about a bill of divorce that lacked enough witnesses. He told them to go and complete the signatures even with a slave picked up from the market.
09.missing: The details of who came and why; the Hebrew says only 'when they came before Rabbi Ami' (the translation supplies the case).

10.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
10.event: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders, reclining in the upper room of the house of Nitza in Lod, were asked whether study or action is greater.
10.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study.
10.outcome: All agreed that study is greater because study leads to action.
10.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in an upper room in Lod when someone asked them whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action; Rabbi Akiva answered study. In the end they all agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.

12.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha.
12.turn: The case came before the Sages to decide whether all of them restricted carrying.
12.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his place of residence renders carrying prohibited.
12.summary: Rabbi Yehuda tells of ben Nappaha, who had houses in five courtyards in Usha. The question of whether each of them affected carrying in its courtyard came before the Sages. They ruled that only the place where he actually lived made carrying without an eiruv forbidden.

13.actor: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and a daughter seeking support
13.event: Someone came before Rav Yosef about a daughter's sustenance from her late father's estate, and he told the sons to give it to her from the dates on the drying mats.
13.turn: Abaye objected that not even a creditor could collect from orphans' movable property.
13.outcome: Rav Yosef clarified that he meant dates still on the tree, fit for the mats, and when pressed further, dates that still needed the palm, so they counted as land.
13.summary: A case came to Rav Yosef about a daughter who needed support from her dead father's estate, and he told the heirs to give her from the dates laid out on mats. Abaye challenged him: would he let even a creditor collect from orphans' movable goods like that? Rav Yosef explained he meant dates ripe enough for the mats but still attached, and when Abaye pressed again, dates that still needed the tree, which count as land rather than movables.

14.actor: Rav Mordekhai, Mar bar Rav Ashi, and Rav Ashi
14.event: A dispute over whether a child's gift is valid was sent to Rav Mordekhai with the attributions reversed, so that Mar bar Rav Ashi seemed to say it is not valid.
14.turn: Rav Mordekhai recalled that Rav Ashi, Mar's father, standing with one foot on the ground and one on the step, had ruled the child's gift valid.
14.outcome: He sent back word to Mar bar Rav Ashi that the gift is valid in every case, large or small, deathbed or healthy.
14.summary: Rav Yeimar and Mar bar Rav Ashi disagreed about whether a young child's gift is valid, but the report reached Rav Mordekhai with their names reversed. Rav Mordekhai sent word to Mar bar Rav Ashi reminding him of what had happened: his father Rav Ashi, standing with one foot on the ground and one on the step, was asked the question and answered that such a gift is valid in all cases.

16.event: A woman seized a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract and also demanded sustenance.
16.turn: She came before Rava for judgment.
16.outcome: Rava told the orphans to give her sustenance, disregarding Rabbi Shimon's view that partial payment counts as full.
16.summary: A widow took a silver cup toward her marriage settlement and still demanded to be supported from the estate. She brought the case to Rava, who told her late husband's orphans to go and give her sustenance, since no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view on this point.

17.actor: Rabbi Hanina Kara and Rabbi Yannai
17.event: Rabbi Hanina Kara sat before Rabbi Yannai and declared that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
17.outcome: He told him to go out and recite his verses outside, since the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda.
17.summary: Rabbi Hanina the Bible reciter was sitting before Rabbi Yannai and announced that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai sent him out, telling him to go recite his verses outside, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

18.event: Rav arrived at the house of bar Shafei Halla and examined the family.
18.summary: Rav once visited the family of bar Shafei Halla and had them examined. The Gemara cites this only to ask what he was examining, and answers that he told people to check whether the family would fall silent in a quarrel, a sign of good lineage.
18.missing: What the examination found and how the visit ended; the incident is only cited in a legal question.

19.actor: Ravina and his host in Mehoza
19.event: Ravina came to Mehoza, and his host showed him a slaughtering knife; Ravina told him to take it to Rava.
19.turn: The host objected that Rava himself says a scholar may examine a knife for himself.
19.outcome: Ravina answered that since he was only buying the meat, it did not count as slaughtering for himself.
19.summary: Ravina visited Mehoza, Rava's town, and his host showed him a knife to check before slaughtering. Ravina told him to take it to Rava. The host asked whether Ravina did not accept Rava's rule that a scholar may check a knife for himself; Ravina replied that he was only buying meat from the host, so the rule did not apply.

20.actor: The people of Neharde'a, and Rav Nahman
20.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
20.turn: In the end wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
20.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions return to their owners.
20.summary: A drought struck Neharde'a and everyone sold their mansions to buy food. Then a wheat shipment arrived, and the sales turned out to have been needless. Rav Nahman ruled that by law the houses went back to their original owners.
